lead: An AR display must show the real world and a computer-made object in one view, lined up in 3D and fast enough to follow the head. Three mechanisms do this: optical see-through (real and virtual light enter through a combiner), video see-through (a camera films the world and graphics are mixed into the picture), and projection (virtual light falls on the real surface). Headsets, phones and table-top rigs choose one. The choice fixes delay, brightness, field of view, occlusion, safety and cost, so it is the first hardware decision.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the three AR requirements, and Unit 3 for head-mounted and stereoscopic displays.

blocks.text: Every AR display must put two light patterns on the retina: light from the real scene and light from the computer image. Only three mechanisms exist.

Send both as light. The computer image is collimated by the display optics and reflected into the eye by a combiner, while real light passes straight through that same combiner. This is optical see-through, worn on the head.

Send both as pixels. A camera captures the real scene, software draws the virtual object into that picture, and a screen shows the single mixed image. This is video see-through. A phone held up at a sofa is the commonest daily example.
Send the virtual light to the object. A projector paints the image onto the real surface. This is projection AR; the user wears nothing.

A fourth arrangement, monitor-based AR, puts the mixed picture on a desktop screen. Nobody looks through it, so it is not registered to one person's eye; it suits design review, surgical planning and classroom teaching.
Some syllabi call the first two "optical and video see-through displays".

sections.h3: Optical see-through: real light through a combiner

blocks.text: The combiner. A half-silvered mirror, also called a beam splitter, sits at 45° in front of the eye, with the microdisplay to the side. Light from the microdisplay reflects off the mirror into the eye, while room light passes straight through. Both reach the retina along the same line of sight.

The waveguide. A thin flat glass plate carries the image by total internal reflection. Light enters at the edge, bounces inside the glass, and a grating on the surface pushes it out towards the pupil. The plate looks like ordinary spectacle glass.
Real light is never turned into a picture, so the real view has no camera delay, resolution limit or noise. Four costs remain.

items: Brightness: the combiner transmits only part of the real light and reflects only part of the virtual light, so both images arrive dimmer than they left the source.
Fixed focus: the virtual image is focused at a fixed distance, often infinity or about 2 m, whatever distance the object claims to be at.

Eye offset: the eye sits about 15–25 mm behind the optics (the eye relief) and slightly below the optical axis, so the virtual image is drawn from a point that is not the eye centre, and registration must be calibrated per user, including interpupillary distance.
No occlusion: in a plain combiner design a virtual object cannot hide a real one, because real light keeps arriving through the combiner.

sections.h3: Video see-through: one picture from a camera

blocks.text: Two small cameras on the front of the headset capture the scene. The renderer draws the virtual object into each frame using the pose from the tracker (see 6.3), and two screens show the result, one per eye. The eye sees only the screens, so real and virtual parts are formed by one pipeline.

That single pipeline gives video see-through its power. The camera frame can be held back until the render is ready, so both parts carry the same delay and stay aligned; otherwise a fast head turn makes the virtual object slide off the real one. Depth from the two cameras, or from SLAM, lets the renderer cut away hidden parts, so a real cup in front of a virtual machine hides it correctly.

The price is paid in four places. The cameras sit a few centimetres from the eyes, so the camera view is not the eye view (parallax, worst for near objects). The camera and render add delay in series. The world looks like a photograph, limited by screen brightness and resolution. And if the camera or power fails, the wearer is blind.
Phone AR is the same method at hand scale: the rear camera films the room, the screen shows the mix, and your hand supplies the window.

In any head-worn fixed-focus display, including both see-through types, the eyes turn inward (vergence) to meet at the distance of the virtual object, while the optics focus that image at a fixed distance (accommodation). The brain receives two conflicting depth cues, which brings eye strain and double images after some minutes. It is the main reason optical designs are hard. Projection AR does not suffer from it because the image is focused on the real surface.

sections.h3: Projection AR, and choosing between them

blocks.text: Spatial projection AR uses a projector fixed in the room and calibrated to a surface: a workbench, a wall, a machine casing. The image lands on the object, and every worker sees it without holding a device. Handheld and body-worn projection carries the projector in the hand or on the shoulder, so the surface is chosen at the moment; some syllabi list this under mobile projection interfaces.

Projection fails in ways a headset does not. The user's hand, arm or body stops the beam. The surface must be pale and matte, because a dark or shiny object reflects light away. Strong room light washes the image out. Calibration must map projector pixels onto the real surface.

figure.caption: The camera capture, the first bar of the top lane, is the extra 33 ms the optical path never pays. The bars end at 68 ms and 20 ms, so at a 60°/s head turn the video view misregisters 4.08° (10.7 cm at 1.5 m) against 1.20° (3.1 cm), 3.4 times worse.

spec.aria: Timeline of AR display delay: the video see-through lane runs capture 0 to 33 ms, pose 33 to 53 ms and display 53 to 68 ms, ending at 68 ms, while the optical see-through lane ends at 20 ms; at 60 degrees per second these give 4.08 degrees and 1.20 degrees of misregistration.

examples.question: A video see-through headset takes 33 ms to capture a frame, 20 ms to compute pose, and 15 ms to display the composited frame. An optical see-through unit needs 20 ms of tracking and display delay. The head turns at 60 degrees per second. Find the misregistration angle and the apparent shift at 1.5 m for each path, and the ratio.
examples.answer: The video path misregisters by 4.08° and shifts the object 10.7 cm at 1.5 m; the optical path misregisters by 1.20° and shifts it 3.1 cm, so the video path is 3.4 times worse until the camera frame is delayed to match the render.
examples.check:
import math
cap = 33.0
pose = 20.0
disp = 15.0
omega = 60.0
d = 1.5
t_video = (cap + pose + disp) / 1000.0
t_opt = pose / 1000.0
ang_v = omega * t_video
ang_o = omega * t_opt
shift_v = d * math.tan(math.radians(ang_v))
shift_o = d * math.tan(math.radians(ang_o))
print(round(t_video * 1000, 1))
print(round(ang_v, 2))
print(round(shift_v * 100, 1))
print(round(ang_o, 2))
print(round(shift_o * 100, 1))
print(round(t_video / t_opt, 1))

traps: Swapping the two see-through types: optical uses a combiner and no camera; video uses a camera and a screen.
Saying video see-through is simply better. It can draw occlusion and match latency, but adds camera delay, camera–eye parallax, and blindness if the camera fails.
Forgetting matched-latency compositing works by delaying the camera frame to the render time. It raises total delay but removes relative slip.
Confusing projection shadow, where the user's body blocks the beam, with occlusion, where a real object correctly hides a virtual one.
Unit slips: turn rate in degrees per second × delay in seconds gives degrees; multiply the metre shift by 100 before quoting centimetres.

quiz.q: Name the three routes by which an AR display can put real and virtual light in front of the eye, and state which one needs no eyewear.
quiz.a: Optical see-through (a combiner in front of the eye), video see-through (a camera and a screen), and projection AR. Projection needs no eyewear.

quiz.q: What is a combiner and what does it do?
quiz.a: A half-silvered mirror or waveguide in front of the eye. It reflects the microdisplay image into the pupil and lets real light pass through, so both images arrive along the same line of sight.

quiz.q: Why can a basic optical see-through display not hide a real object behind a virtual one?
quiz.a: In a basic combiner design real light is never captured, so there is no depth map and no way to switch the real scene off. The combiner keeps transmitting room light, so the real object shines through the virtual one. Switchable shutters or per-pixel dimming can add partial occlusion.

quiz.q: Why is matched-latency compositing needed in video see-through?
quiz.a: The camera stream and the rendered stream are produced at different times. If the camera frame is shown immediately while the render lags, the two parts come from different head poses and the virtual object slides off the real one. Holding the camera frame until the render is ready gives both streams the same delay, so they stay aligned.

quiz.q: An optical see-through unit has 25 ms of tracking and display delay. The head turns at 40 degrees per second and the virtual object is at 2 m. Find the misregistration angle and the apparent shift.

A factory wants step-by-step assembly guidance drawn on a large dark metal casing, with several workers viewing at once and no devices worn. Which display route fits, and what two problems must be solved?
quiz.a: Projection AR with a fixed spatial projector, because it needs no eyewear and serves many viewers. Problem one: dark metal reflects little light, so the surface must be treated or a brighter projector used. Problem two: the workers' bodies block the beam, and the projector must be calibrated to the casing geometry.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is pushing the combiner into thin high-index waveguides with micro-LED or laser-scanning light engines, which raise field of view and brightness while the plate still looks like ordinary spectacles. Occlusion-capable optical see-through is an open research problem: switchable liquid-crystal shutters and per-pixel dimming can block real light exactly where the virtual object is drawn. Projector–camera systems already guide assembly on factory benches. Retinal scanning displays, which draw the image with a scanned beam straight onto the retina, try to sidestep the fixed-focus problem. Search for "waveguide combiner", "switchable occlusion see-through" and "projector–camera calibration".
